# Post-Training: Adaptation and Alignment {#sec-post-training}

@sec-pretraining ended with a model that had read the web and could
not be spoken to. This chapter is about the second and third stages: the ones
that are cheap, that you can actually run, and that decide almost everything a
user will notice.

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain why a base model answers a question with another question, and what
  supervised fine-tuning changes so that it stops;
- write a training example in chat-template form and say which tokens the loss
  is computed on and why the rest are masked;
- work out, from a model's `config.json` alone, how many parameters a LoRA
  adapter adds and how much GPU memory the run will need;
- distinguish SFT, RLHF, DPO, and GRPO by the data each one demands, not by
  the acronym;
- choose between prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and distillation with an
  explicit decision rule;
- detect catastrophic forgetting by evaluating the same model, on the same
  held-out benchmark, before and after.

## The model that answers a different question {#sec-base-model-failure}

Here is the entire problem in one exchange. You have a base model — the raw
output of stage 1, nothing else done to it. You type:

```text
What is the capital of Turkey?
```

and it continues:

```text
What is the capital of France?
What is the capital of Germany?
What is the largest city in Turkey?
```

Nothing has gone wrong. [The model did exactly what it was trained to do, and
that is the problem]{.hl}. It was trained on one objective — *given this text,
what text usually comes next* — and on the open web, a line that looks like a
quiz question is followed, far more often than not, by another quiz question.
It is completing a worksheet. It has no idea that you wanted it to stop and
turn around and address you.

::: {.column-margin}
Try this yourself: on the Hub, models named `Llama-3.1-8B` and
`Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` are the same pretraining run. The first is the base
model. The second has been through the two stages in this chapter. The
difference in behaviour is enormous; the difference in cost is large but not
published for these two models. For scale, InstructGPT's own figures put SFT
plus PPO at 64.9 petaflop/s-days against 3,640 for pretraining — about 1.8%, or a
factor of 56, before the reward model and everything around it.
:::

Ask the same base model a factual question it certainly knows, and phrase it as
a sentence to be finished — `The capital of Turkey is` — and it will answer
correctly. So the knowledge is present. What is missing is not information. It
is a *convention*: that a question addressed to you is a request for an answer
from you.

This is worth being precise about, because it sets up everything that follows.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Four things you might be missing, and only one of them is fixed by training
on more text.**

| what is missing | symptom | what fixes it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **knowledge** | confidently wrong about your documents, your prices, last week | retrieval (@sec-rag) |
| **format** | right content, wrong shape: prose where you needed JSON | prompting, constrained decoding |
| **behaviour** | answers the wrong *kind* of question; wrong register; will not refuse | fine-tuning (this chapter) |
| **cost** | correct, but too slow or too expensive per call | distillation, quantization |

Most fine-tuning projects that fail are attempts to fix row 1 with the
technique from row 3.
:::

We will come back to that table at the end and turn it into a decision tree.
First, the machinery.

**What we will look at.** Why a pretrained model answers the wrong question,
and the sequence of stages that fixes it. Then each stage in turn, with the
cheap version alongside the expensive one: supervised fine-tuning and its
parameter-efficient cousin, preference optimization, feedback that is not
human, and distillation. Finally, the two questions that matter more than any
of them — when *not* to fine-tune, and what the model quietly forgets when you
do.

## What the stages actually do {#sec-stage-anatomy}

@sec-pretraining drew the three stages by scale. Here is the same
pipeline drawn by *mechanism*: what each stage puts in, what signal it
optimizes, and which weights it is allowed to touch.

::: {.fig-cap}
The column that matters is the third one. Pretraining scores *what came next in
the corpus*; SFT scores *what should come next in the answer*; preference
tuning scores *which of two answers is better*. Only the last of those cannot
be written down as a target string — which is exactly why it needs a different
algorithm.
:::
::::

Notice what stages 2 and 3 have in common: neither one is where the model's
knowledge of the world mostly comes from. That is not a claim that supervised
fine-tuning *cannot* teach facts — it demonstrably can, and continued
pretraining on domain text is a standard way to add some. The claim is about
scale and reliability: a stage-2 run touching a few million tokens cannot
broadly or dependably revise a world model built from millions of times
more text (15.6 trillion tokens against a few million), and [when people reach for it as their knowledge-update mechanism,
that is precisely when fine-tuning disappoints]{.hl}. @sec-rag exists because
retrieval is the mechanism that does that job.

## Supervised fine-tuning {#sec-sft}

### One example, in full

A [supervised fine-tuning](#gloss-supervised-fine-tuning){#term-supervised-fine-tuning .term-ref}
example is a prompt and the response you wish the model had given.
That is the whole idea. The difficulty is entirely in the details of how it is
written down, and two of those details break runs silently.

::: {#gloss-supervised-fine-tuning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**supervised fine-tuning** — training on prompt-and-answer pairs with the
ordinary next-token loss, computed on the answer alone. The same objective as
pretraining; a different choice of which text it is applied to.
[↩](#term-supervised-fine-tuning){.term-back}
:::

Here is a single Turkish example as it exists in a JSONL file:

```text
{"messages": [
  {"role": "user",      "content": "Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? 'Kargo çok hızlı geldi, teşekkürler.'"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "Olumlu."}
]}
```

Before the model sees it, that structure is flattened into a single token
sequence by the model's [chat template](#gloss-chat-template){#term-chat-template .term-ref} — a
string template shipped with the tokenizer, different for every model family:

::: {#gloss-chat-template .column-margin .term-gloss}
**chat template** — the exact string format, including special marker tokens,
that a chat model was fine-tuned on. It lives in the tokenizer, not the model,
and using the wrong one degrades quality quietly rather than raising an error.
[↩](#term-chat-template){.term-back}
:::

```text
<|begin_of_text|><|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>

Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? 'Kargo çok hızlı geldi, teşekkürler.'<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Olumlu.<|eot_id|>
```

Those `<|...|>` markers are real tokens with real embeddings. They are how the
model knows where its turn begins — and therefore how it knows to *answer*
rather than continue. The behaviour change we are after is, mechanically,
mostly the model learning what follows the assistant header token.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Never hand-write the template.** Call
`tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)` and print the result
once. Every model family uses different markers, and a template mismatch
between training and serving quietly degrades quality with no error message
anywhere — quietly enough that people spend weeks blaming the data. This is the single most common way an
otherwise correct fine-tune underperforms.

At inference, call it with `add_generation_prompt=True`: that appends the
empty assistant header, which is the model's cue that it is now its turn to
answer. Forget it and even a well-tuned chat model may simply continue the
user's message.
:::

### Loss masking: the detail that silently breaks runs

Now the second detail. The sequence above is, say, 46 tokens long. Six of them
are the answer. On which tokens do you compute the loss?

If you say *all of them* — which is what you get if you naively reuse the
pretraining objective — then 40 of your 46 gradient signals are teaching the
model **to generate the prompt**. You are training a question generator that
occasionally emits an answer.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Loss masking: which tokens the gradient is allowed to come from</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 268" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="Two rows of token boxes over the same sequence. The top row, labelled wrong, shades every token including the user prompt, with a note saying forty of forty-six gradient signals teach the model to write the prompt. The bottom row, labelled right, shades only the six assistant response tokens and greys the rest, with a note saying only the response contributes to the loss. Both rows show the same token sequence: a header marker, the Turkish question, an assistant header marker, the word Olumlu, and an end-of-turn marker.">
  <text x="14" y="22" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">THE SAME 46-TOKEN SEQUENCE, TWO CHOICES OF LOSS MASK</text>

  <text x="14" y="60" class="t-xs t-b t-rose">✗ loss on everything</text>
  <rect x="14" y="72" width="120" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="74" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">user header</text>
  <rect x="140" y="72" width="330" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="305" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? …</text>
  <rect x="476" y="72" width="136" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="544" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">assistant header</text>
  <rect x="618" y="72" width="76" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="656" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">Olumlu.</text>
  <rect x="700" y="72" width="50" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="725" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">eot</text>
  <text x="14" y="122" class="t-xs t-rose">40 of 46 gradient signals teach the model to write the question.</text>

  <text x="14" y="168" class="t-xs t-b t-accent">✓ loss on the response only</text>
  <rect x="14" y="180" width="120" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="74" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">user header</text>
  <rect x="140" y="180" width="330" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="305" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? …</text>
  <rect x="476" y="180" width="136" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="544" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">assistant header</text>
  <rect x="618" y="180" width="76" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="656" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-b">Olumlu.</text>
  <rect x="700" y="180" width="50" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="725" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-b">eot</text>
  <text x="14" y="230" class="t-xs t-muted">Masked tokens are still read — they are the context. They just do not produce gradient.</text>
  <text x="14" y="252" class="t-xs t-b">Set the label of every masked position to −100 and the loss function skips it.</text>
</svg>
```
::: {.fig-cap}
Masking is not about hiding the prompt from the model. The model still attends
to every prompt token; that is what conditioning *means*. Masking only decides
which positions are allowed to say “you should have predicted something else
here”.
:::
::::

In practice you build a `labels` tensor that is a copy of `input_ids` with
every non-response position set to `-100`, the value PyTorch's cross-entropy
treats as *ignore*. Modern SFT libraries do this for you if you tell them
where the response starts; the failure mode is reaching for a plain causal-LM
training loop and forgetting. Two related details. Do not shift the labels one
position yourself: Hugging Face causal-LM models already compare the prediction
at position $t$ with the label at $t+1$ internally, and shifting twice trains
the model to predict two tokens ahead. And in a multi-turn conversation the
usual choice is to keep the loss on *every* assistant turn and mask every user
turn, not just the last exchange.

::: {.column-margin}
There is one legitimate reason to train on prompt tokens: if your prompts are
themselves in a domain the base model has never seen, the extra signal helps
the model learn the language of that domain. It is a deliberate choice, and it should be
justified in your run notes rather than inherited from a copied script.
:::

### How many examples do you actually need?

The honest answer is that the field's own numbers span three orders of
magnitude, and the spread is informative rather than embarrassing.

| project | SFT examples | what they were for |
|:--|--:|:--|
| LIMA [@zhou2023lima] | 1,000 | showing that a *little* is enough |
| InstructGPT [@ouyang2022training] | 12,725 prompts | a general-purpose assistant |
| Self-Instruct [@wang2023selfinstruct] | ~52,000 instructions | synthetic data; only 175 human-written seed tasks |
| Tülu 3 [@lambert2025tulu3] | 939,344 prompts | a competitive open recipe |

That last row hides the real work. Tülu 3's team assembled **23,327,961**
candidate prompts and kept 939,344 of them for supervised fine-tuning — under
one in twenty-four — with a further 425,145 routed to preference tuning
[@lambert2025tulu3]. The published artefact is a filtering decision far more
than it is a collection effort.

LIMA is the interesting entry. Its authors fine-tuned a 65B LLaMa on exactly
1,000 curated prompt-response pairs — 750 harvested from community Q&A sites
(Stack Exchange, wikiHow, Reddit), 250 written or adapted by the authors — with *no* reinforcement learning and *no*
preference modelling at all. Against GPT-4, human raters judged LIMA's answers
equal or better 43% of the time; against Bard 58%, against the RLHF-trained
DaVinci003 65% [@zhou2023lima].

There is a second reason a small set can go so far, shown in 2021 by the FLAN
work, before LIMA: a model fine-tuned on a *collection* of instruction-phrased tasks improves on
tasks it never saw during that fine-tune [@wei2022finetuned]. What SFT installs
is not a list of answers but the habit of treating an instruction as one.

The LIMA authors' explanation is what they call the **Superficial Alignment
Hypothesis**: essentially all of a model's knowledge and capability is acquired
during pretraining, and alignment mainly teaches it *which sub-distribution of
formats to use* when interacting with users. If that is right, then a thousand
examples is plenty to specify a format — and no amount of examples would be
enough to install knowledge that pretraining did not.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The practical reading.** Below roughly a thousand well-made examples, you are
still buying format. Between one thousand and fifty thousand, you are buying
coverage of the *variety* of inputs you will see. Above that you are buying
robustness on the long tail, and the marginal example is worth much less than
the marginal *hour of quality control* on the examples you already have.

Both LIMA and Tülu 3 spent most of their effort on curation, not collection.
:::

## Parameter-efficient tuning {#sec-lora}

Everything so far assumed you can run the training step at all. For anything
above about a billion parameters, on the hardware you are likely to have, you
cannot — and the reason is not the model.

### Where the memory actually goes

Count the bytes one parameter costs during mixed-precision AdamW training in
the configuration mainstream stacks default to — bf16 compute with an fp32
master copy and fp32 optimizer moments. Other configurations exist and cost
differently: 8-bit optimizer states, fused fp32-free schemes and sharded
optimizers all change this table. The 16 is a default, not a law.

| what is stored | bytes per parameter | why it exists |
|:--|--:|:--|
| bf16 weight | 2 | the model itself |
| bf16 gradient | 2 | one per **trainable** parameter |
| fp32 master weight | 4 | bf16 has too few mantissa bits to accumulate tiny updates |
| fp32 Adam $m$ | 4 | running mean of the gradient |
| fp32 Adam $v$ | 4 | running mean of the gradient *squared* |
| **total, trainable** | **16** | |
| **total, frozen** | **2** | a weight you never update only has to be read |

::: {.column-margin}
The fp32 master copy is the least obvious row and the one people try to delete
first. Without it, an update of size $10^{-5}$ added to a weight of size $1$
rounds straight back to $1$ in bf16 — while fp32 keeps it, as 1.00001 — and the
training silently stalls. Pick the example carefully: $10^{-8}$ would vanish in
fp32 as well, since single precision has about seven decimal digits. Keeping
one high-precision copy of the weights is what makes low-precision training
work at all.
:::

Read the two totals against each other. [The model itself is one eighth of the
bill. Optimizer state — the three fp32 rows — is three quarters of it, and the
gradient is the remaining eighth.]{.hl} That ratio is the whole of
[parameter-efficient fine-tuning](#gloss-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning){#term-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning .term-ref}
(PEFT): freeze a parameter and *seven* of its eight
instalments disappear, leaving only the bf16 weight you still have to read.

::: {#gloss-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** — the family LoRA belongs to: train
a small fraction of the weights (or a few added ones) and leave the rest
frozen. Usually written *PEFT*.
[↩](#term-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning){.term-back}
:::

The arithmetic is checkable against a published figure. QLoRA states that
16-bit fine-tuning of a 65B LLaMA "requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory"
[@dettmers2023qlora]. Where does 780 come from?

$$
65 \times 10^9 \;\text{params} \times 12 \;\text{bytes} = 780 \;\text{GB}
$$

Twelve bytes per parameter — and the paper does not say which twelve. The
natural reading against the table above is the three fp32 rows, master weight,
$m$ and $v$, with the bf16 weight and gradient pushing the real requirement to
$65 \times 16 = 1{,}040$ GB and so justifying "more than". A second reading
fits the same twelve exactly: bf16 weight, bf16 gradient, fp32 $m$, fp32 $v$,
no master copy, with "more than" absorbing activations instead. [Either
decomposition lands on the same conclusion — the headline number is dominated
by state that exists only because the parameter is being trained.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
Reconstructing a published memory figure is worth doing precisely because it
usually has more than one solution. Papers report totals, not itemisations; you
infer the itemisation from the total, and honesty requires saying which one you
assumed.
:::

The LoRA paper's figure moves in the other direction: on GPT-3 175B, training
VRAM falls "from 1.2TB to 350GB" [@hu2022lora]. The endpoint is clean —

$$
175 \times 10^9 \times 2\;\text{bytes} = 350\;\text{GB}
$$

is the frozen bf16 weights *and nothing else*. The starting point is not.
1.2 TB across 175B parameters is about 6.9 bytes each, well under the 16 the
table predicts, so that figure was measured under a setup the paper does not
spell out. Only cheaper per-parameter state gets you there — 8-bit or 16-bit
optimizer moments, or no fp32 master copy. Sharding across many cards and
activation checkpointing do not: sharding spreads the same bytes over more
GPUs, and checkpointing trims activations, not the per-parameter state. Quote the 350 GB as arithmetic you can
reproduce, and the 1.2 TB as *their* measurement.

### The low-rank hypothesis

So we want to freeze the weights. But a frozen model does not learn. The
question is what you can add on the side that is small enough to be cheap and
expressive enough to be useful.

[LoRA](#gloss-lora){#term-lora .term-ref}'s answer starts from an observation about what fine-tuning does. A
pretrained weight matrix $W_0$ is a general-purpose feature map, built from
trillions of tokens covering every domain at once. The change you need for
*one* task is not general-purpose. It is a specific, narrow adjustment. The
hypothesis [@hu2022lora] is that this adjustment $\Delta W$, while it is a
full $d \times k$ matrix in shape, carries far less information than its shape
suggests — it has **low intrinsic rank**.

If that is true, you can write it as a product of two thin matrices:

$$
W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \qquad r \ll \min(d,k)
$$

::: {#gloss-lora .column-margin .term-gloss}
**LoRA** — low-rank adaptation: freezing a pretrained weight matrix and
learning a small pair of matrices whose product is added to it. The pair has
$r(d+k)$ parameters instead of $dk$, and at inference it can be folded back
into the original weight so nothing gets slower.
[↩](#term-lora){.term-back}
:::

Count what that saves. For one of Llama 3.1 8B's $4096 \times 4096$ query
projections, $\Delta W$ in full has $16{,}777{,}216$ parameters. At $r = 8$,
$BA$ has $8 \times (4096 + 4096) = 65{,}536$ — **256 times fewer**, for the
same output shape.

### What $A$ and $B$ actually hold

The two matrices are not symmetric in role, and the asymmetry is the part
worth understanding.

::: {.fig-cap}
Follow the detour from $x$ to $h$ and the two matrices have distinct jobs: $A$
projects the input down to $r$ numbers — it decides *which few directions of
the input this task cares about*. $B$ projects those $r$ numbers back up — it
decides *what to write into the output* for each direction $A$ found.
:::
::::

That reading also explains the initialisation, which looks arbitrary until you
ask what happens otherwise:

| $A$ init | $B$ init | what happens |
|:--|:--|:--|
| zero | zero | $BA = 0$ forever: both gradients are proportional to the other matrix, so nothing ever leaves zero |
| random | random | $BA \neq 0$ at step 0, so training *begins* by injecting noise into a carefully pretrained model |
| **random** | **zero** | $BA = 0$ at step 0 but $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial B \neq 0$: the run starts exactly at the pretrained model and moves from there |
| zero | random | also $BA = 0$ at step 0, and $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial A \neq 0$: this escapes too |

Two of the four work, not one. Both of the bottom rows start the adapted model
exactly at the pretrained model *and* have somewhere to go, because the
gradient with respect to each matrix is proportional to the *other* one — so
you only need one of the pair to be non-zero. [What matters is the product,
not which factor carries the randomness.]{.hl}

LoRA takes the third row: "a random Gaussian initialization for $A$ and zero
for $B$" [@hu2022lora]. The paper states the convention and does not argue for
it over the fourth row, and neither will this book. What the $B = 0$
initialisation buys is that the adapter leaves the pretrained model untouched at
step 0: you start from a model that already works, where random–random
initialisation would start the run from noise.

### Rank and alpha, and why there are two knobs

The update is not added raw. It is scaled by $\alpha / r$, where $\alpha$ is a
constant you choose [@hu2022lora]:

$$
h = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x
$$

The stated purpose of the division is practical rather than theoretical. The
authors write that the scaling "helps to reduce the need to retune
hyperparameters when we vary $r$" [@hu2022lora] — that is, it is there so a
rank sweep stays a rank sweep instead of silently becoming a learning-rate
sweep at the same time. Without it, every change to $r$ would perturb the
effective step size on the adapter path, and you could not tell which knob
produced the change in your metric.

Which leaves $\alpha$ doing one job, and the paper says exactly what that job
is: "tuning $\alpha$ is roughly the same as tuning the learning rate"
[@hu2022lora]. It is a fixed multiplier on the whole adapter path, so the
widespread convention $\alpha = 2r$ means nothing more exotic than "scale the
adapter by 2".

That convention is the community's, not the authors'. They report setting
$\alpha$ "to the first $r$ we try" and then leaving it alone. In other words,
they did not tune it. Note also that this is *not* $\alpha = r$ at every rank:
if you fix $\alpha$ at 8 because you tried $r = 8$ first, then $r = 16$ runs
at $\alpha/r = 0.5$. [Treat $\alpha = 2r$ as a default someone else picked for you, not
as a result.]{.hl}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Two knobs, two questions.**

- **$r$** asks *how much capacity does this adaptation need?* Raise it when
  the task is far from anything in pretraining — a new language, a new
  notation, a genuinely new output format.
- **$\alpha$** asks *how hard should the adapter push?* Raise it when training
  is underfitting and lower it when the model has started producing
  confident nonsense.

They are commonly conflated because $\alpha = 2r$ makes them move together.
Break the convention when you sweep, or you are sweeping one knob and calling
it two.
:::

### The arithmetic of an adapter

A LoRA adapter on a $d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}$ matrix adds exactly
$r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})$ parameters. Everything else is bookkeeping:
which matrices you attach to, and how many layers there are.

The three configurations below were computed from each model's own
`config.json`, so they are what you would actually get:

| model | targets | $r$ | trainable | share of model |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| BERTurk base (110.6M, 12 layers) | query, value | 8 | 294,912 | 0.267% |
| | + key, output | 8 | 589,824 | 0.533% |
| | + the MLP | 8 | 1,327,104 | 1.200% |
| Llama 3.1 8B (32 layers, $d$=4096) | q_proj, v_proj | 8 | 3,407,872 | 0.042% |
| | all attention | 8 | 6,815,744 | 0.085% |
| | attention + MLP | 8 | 20,971,520 | 0.261% |
| Qwen 2.5 7B (28 layers, $d$=3584) | q_proj, v_proj | 8 | 2,523,136 | 0.033% |
| | attention + MLP | 8 | 20,185,088 | 0.265% |

::: {.column-margin}
LoRA is not the only parameter-efficient method, only the one that won. Prompt
tuning [@lester2021power] trains a handful of *virtual tokens* prepended to the
input and touches no weight at all — it becomes competitive with full
fine-tuning as the model grows, and it is worth knowing about as the extreme
end of the same idea.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Qwen's `q_proj, v_proj` adapters come to 2.52M against Llama's 3.41M, and it is
tempting to credit grouped-query attention (@sec-attention-cost) — Qwen 2.5 7B
uses 4 key-value heads to Llama's 8, making `v_proj` a $3584 \times 512$ matrix
rather than $4096 \times 1024$. Give Qwen 8 KV heads and the count rises to
2.64M, so GQA is only about 13% of the 884,736-parameter gap. The rest is
$d = 3584$ against 4096, over 28 layers against 32.
:::

Two things fall out. First, **the MLP is most of the model**, and adding it to
an attention-only adapter is the single largest jump on the table: 2.25× on
BERTurk, 3.08× on Llama. Measured from `q_proj, v_proj` alone the jump is
larger still — 4.5× on BERTurk, 6.2× on Llama, 8.0× on Qwen. Second, even the
most generous setting here is under 0.3% of an 8B model. Rank spans a wider
range than targets do — $r$ from 1 to 128 is a factor of 128 — yet even the
top of that range stays well under one percent of the model:

| $r$ | 1 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| trainable (q,v only) | 425,984 | 1.70M | 3.41M | 6.82M | 13.6M | 27.3M | 54.5M |
| share of Llama 3.1 8B | 0.005% | 0.021% | 0.042% | 0.085% | 0.170% | 0.340% | 0.679% |

Even at $r = 128$ you are training two thirds of one percent of the model.

### Work out your own run

The arithmetic above is for one configuration. Yours will differ, and the
numbers move faster than intuition does — so rather than trusting a rule of
thumb, put your own model size and rank in and read the memory off.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraN = Inputs.range([0.1, 405], { value: 8.03, step: 0.01, label: "Model size (billions of parameters)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraShare = Inputs.range([0.005, 5], { value: 0.52, step: 0.005, label: "Adapter size (% of model)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraMode = Inputs.select(
  ["full fine-tune", "LoRA (bf16 base)", "QLoRA (4-bit base)"],
  { value: "LoRA (bf16 base)", label: "Method" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
loraCalc = {
  const N = loraN * 1e9;
  const trainable = loraMode === "full fine-tune" ? N : N * loraShare / 100;
  const frozen = N - trainable;
  const baseBytes = loraMode.startsWith("QLoRA") ? 0.5 : 2;
  const bytes = frozen * baseBytes + trainable * 16;
  const gib = bytes / 2 ** 30;
  const cards = [16, 24, 40, 48, 80, 141];
  const fits = cards.find((g) => gib * 1.35 < g);
  return { trainable, gib, fits, full: (N * 16) / 2 ** 30 };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:0.95rem">
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">trainable parameters</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        loraCalc.trainable >= 1e9
          ? (loraCalc.trainable / 1e9).toFixed(2) + "B"
          : (loraCalc.trainable / 1e6).toFixed(1) + "M"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">weights + gradients + optimizer</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${loraCalc.gib.toFixed(1)} GiB</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">smallest card it plausibly fits on</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        loraCalc.fits ? loraCalc.fits + " GB" : "more than 141 GB"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">versus a full fine-tune</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        (loraCalc.full / loraCalc.gib).toFixed(1)
      }× less</td></tr>
</table>
<p style="font-size:0.85rem; opacity:0.75; margin-top:8px">
Activations and activation gradients are excluded, and at LoRA-sized adapter
counts they are not a rounding error — see the caution below. The "fits on"
column allows 35% headroom for them, which is a convention chosen for this
widget, not a measured constant.</p>`
```

The defaults are Llama 3.1 8B (8.03B parameters) with an $r{=}16$ adapter on
attention and MLP — 41,943,040 parameters, or 0.52% of the model. Full
fine-tune: **119.7 GiB**, past every common 24–80 GB single-GPU configuration
and past the 141 GB H200 only once you add activations at a real batch size. LoRA: **15.5 GiB**, a 24 GB consumer card. QLoRA: **4.3 GiB**, a laptop.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**What this widget leaves out is the part that will surprise you.** It counts
weights, gradients and optimizer state, because those are what LoRA removes.
It does not count activations, and once the optimizer is gone they are what is
left. QLoRA's authors measured it: for a 7B LLaMA at batch size 1, with an
adapter at "commonly used 0.2% of the original model weights", the LoRA *input
gradients* occupy 567 MB while the LoRA *parameters* occupy 26 MB
[@dettmers2023qlora]. [Twenty-two times more memory goes to backpropagating
through the frozen network than to the thing you are training.]{.hl}

This is why gradient checkpointing appears in every serious LoRA recipe, and
why the widget's numbers are a floor rather than an estimate. It is also why
the lab at the end of this chapter measures a much less dramatic ratio than the
arithmetic here predicts.
:::

### QLoRA: quantize the part you are not training

That last step needs one more idea. In the LoRA row above, the 15.5 GiB is now
almost entirely the frozen bf16 base — the adapter's optimizer state is a
rounding error. So squeeze the base.

QLoRA [@dettmers2023qlora] does exactly that, storing frozen weights in a
4-bit format called **NF4** and dequantizing each block back to bf16 only for
the moment it is needed in the forward and backward pass. Three pieces make it
work:

- **4-bit NormalFloat**, a data type whose 16 levels are placed at the
  quantiles of a normal distribution — chosen because trained network weights
  are close to normally distributed, so the levels land where the weights
  actually are;
- **double quantization**, which quantizes the per-block scaling constants
  themselves, because at small block sizes those constants become a
  non-trivial share of the total;
- **paged optimizers**, which let optimizer state spill to CPU memory during the memory spikes that would otherwise kill a long run outright.

The headline result: fine-tuning a 65B model goes from ">780 GB of GPU memory
to &lt;48 GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to
a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline" [@dettmers2023qlora]. Their Guanaco 65B,
trained this way in 24 hours on a single GPU, reached 99.3% of ChatGPT's score
on the 80-question Vicuna benchmark, as scored by GPT-4 acting as judge rather
than by humans.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**"Without degrading" is measured against full fine-tuning, not plain LoRA.**
The paper's claim covers runtime too, but its comparison is a 16-bit *full*
fine-tune. Against plain LoRA, dequantizing every block on every forward and
backward pass costs arithmetic. QLoRA buys you the ability to run at all on a
small card; it does not make the step faster than plain LoRA on a card where
plain LoRA already fits, and usually makes it somewhat slower.
:::

### The payoff nobody mentions until they are on call

LoRA has an operational property that matters more, in a company, than any of
the training savings: an adapter can be **merged back into the base weights**.
Since $h = W_0x + \frac{\alpha}{r}BAx = (W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA)x$, you can
compute that sum once and ship an ordinary model. Serving is exactly as fast
as the original — the paper's "no additional inference latency"
[@hu2022lora], and the reason LoRA displaced the earlier bottleneck adapters
[@houlsby2019parameter], which insert extra layers and therefore extra latency
forever.

Or you can *not* merge, keep the base shared in memory, and swap adapters per
request:

| tenants | one shared base + adapters | a separate 8B copy each | ratio |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | 15.7 GiB | 149.6 GiB | 9.5× |
| 100 | 22.8 GiB | 1,495.7 GiB | 65.7× |
| 1,000 | 93.1 GiB | 14,957.0 GiB | 160.7× |

The adapter size those rows assume is an $r{=}16$ adapter on attention *and*
MLP, saved in bf16: $41{,}943{,}040 \times 2$ bytes, exactly 80 MiB. Change
either choice and the figure moves a long way — `q_proj, v_proj` only at the
same rank is 6.82M parameters, 13 MiB, and `peft` will happily save the same
adapter in fp32 and double whatever you expected. [Always state targets and
dtype when you quote an adapter size]{.hl}; on its own the rank tells you
almost nothing.

Even at the generous end, a thousand customers with a thousand private
fine-tunes fit, together, on one node. This is why "fine-tuning" is a product
at all, rather than a research technique —
and it is worth noticing that the paper made the same point about GPT-3 in
2021: 100 adapted models cost 350 GB + 35 MB × 100 ≈ 354 GB, against 35 TB for
100 separate copies [@hu2022lora].

## Preference optimization {#sec-preference}

### The thing supervised fine-tuning cannot do

Take a question with no single right answer:

```text
Kredi kartı borcumu nasıl kapatabilirim?
(How can I pay off my credit card debt?)
```

There is no target string. There are a thousand acceptable answers and they
differ along axes you can *recognise* but cannot *write down*: too curt, too
long, too confident about your finances, gives advice it should have refused
to give, correct but reads like a pamphlet. Supervised fine-tuning needs a
target string. Here you have none.

But you can still do something: show two candidate answers to a person and ask
which is better. The result is a
[preference pair](#gloss-preference-pair){#term-preference-pair .term-ref}, and
producing one is a much easier judgement than writing the ideal answer — it is
a judgement you can collect at scale from people who could not have written
either answer themselves.

::: {#gloss-preference-pair .column-margin .term-gloss}
**preference pair** — one prompt, two candidate answers, and a label saying
which is better. It carries no information about how good either answer is in
absolute terms, which is exactly why it is cheap to collect.
[↩](#term-preference-pair){.term-back}
:::

[This is the whole reason preference tuning exists as a separate stage.]{.hl}
It is not a better version of SFT. It optimizes a different kind of signal:
one that only exists as a comparison [@christiano2017deep].

### RLHF: the four-model dance

The original recipe,
reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
[@stiennon2020learning; @ouyang2022training], turns those
comparisons into a training signal in two steps: fit a
[reward model](#gloss-reward-model){#term-reward-model .term-ref} to the
preferences, then optimize the language model against it.


Two words from reinforcement learning appear from here on. The **policy** is
simply the model being trained, seen as a rule that picks the next token given
the text so far. The **KL divergence** $\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}[\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}]$
measures how far one probability distribution has moved from another; it is
zero when the two are identical and grows as they separate. Here it measures
how far the policy has drifted from the model it started as.

::: {#gloss-reward-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**reward model** — a model trained on human comparisons that reads a prompt and
an answer and returns one number. It exists to turn *A is better than B* into
something an optimizer can maximise.
[↩](#term-reward-model){.term-back}
:::

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">RLHF, and what has to be in memory at once</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 456" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="A two-phase diagram. Phase one, on the left, shows a prompt producing two candidate answers, a human choosing the better one, and that comparison training a reward model that outputs a single scalar score. Phase two, on the right, shows a training loop with four models resident in memory at once: the policy being trained, a frozen reference copy of it used to compute a KL penalty, the frozen reward model that scores samples, and a value model that estimates expected return. The policy generates a sample, the reward model scores it, the KL term penalises drift from the reference, and PPO updates the policy. A note at the bottom states that four models of comparable size must be held simultaneously, which is the practical objection to RLHF.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="rl-a" viewBox="0 0 8 8" refX="7" refY="4" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0.5 L7.5,4 L0,7.5 z" class="head"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <text x="14" y="22" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">PHASE 1 — LEARN WHAT PEOPLE PREFER</text>
  <rect x="14" y="34" width="336" height="182" rx="10" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="30" y="60" class="t-xs t-mono t-muted">prompt</text>
  <rect x="30" y="70" width="140" height="34" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="100" y="91" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">answer A</text>
  <rect x="184" y="70" width="140" height="34" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="254" y="91" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">answer B</text>
  <text x="177" y="128" class="t-xs t-mid t-b">a person picks one</text>
  <line x1="177" y1="136" x2="177" y2="154" class="ln" marker-end="url(#rl-a)"/>
  <rect x="70" y="158" width="214" height="44" rx="8" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="177" y="177" class="t-xs t-mid t-b t-rose">REWARD MODEL</text>
  <text x="177" y="194" class="t-xs t-mid t-muted">text in, one number out</text>

  <line x1="352" y1="126" x2="376" y2="126" class="ln" marker-end="url(#rl-a)"/>

  <text x="392" y="22" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">PHASE 2 — OPTIMIZE AGAINST IT</text>
  <rect x="392" y="34" width="358" height="182" rx="10" class="box-accent"/>

```
::: {.fig-cap}
The reward model is the interesting object: it converts an *ordering* — A beat
B — into a *scalar*, which is what a reinforcement-learning algorithm needs.
Everything expensive about RLHF follows from having built that converter and
then needing to keep it, and a frozen reference, and a value estimator, all in
memory while the policy generates. The reinforcement-learning algorithm in the middle is PPO
[@schulman2017ppo], chosen for stability rather than for anything to do with
language.
:::
::::

The result was not marginal. InstructGPT's 1.3B model, put through this
pipeline, produced outputs that human labellers preferred to those of the 175B
GPT-3 — "despite having 100x fewer parameters" [@ouyang2022training]. And the
stage that reversed a hundredfold difference in size was cheap. The authors
report it: training the 175B SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-days and the 175B
PPO-ptx model 60, "compared to 3,640 petaflops/s-days for GPT-3"
[@ouyang2022training]. [The reported SFT and PPO-ptx runs together cost about 1.8% of what pretraining cost, and that total leaves out the reward model.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
That comparison is the strongest single argument in this chapter for taking
post-training seriously. It is also the strongest argument for *not* believing
that parameter count tells you what a model can do.
:::

### DPO: deriving the shortcut away

Look again at the diagram and ask which box is doing indispensable work. The
reward model exists only to score samples during PPO. If the policy's own
probabilities could be read as a reward, the box would be redundant.

They can. This is the
[direct preference optimization](#gloss-direct-preference-optimization){#term-direct-preference-optimization .term-ref}
result [@rafailov2023dpo], and the derivation is worth stating because it is
short and the conclusion is otherwise mystifying.

::: {#gloss-direct-preference-optimization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**direct preference optimization** — training on preference pairs with an
ordinary gradient step, having proved that the reward model in RLHF was never a
separate object. Usually written *DPO*.
[↩](#term-direct-preference-optimization){.term-back}
:::

Before the shortcut, the two objectives it is a shortcut *around*, because the
derivation below leans on both. First, the reward model is fitted to the
comparisons with the **Bradley–Terry** likelihood — the assumption that a person
prefers $y_w$ over $y_l$ with probability $\sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))$. Here
$y_w$ is the preferred (*winning*) answer, $y_l$ the rejected (*losing*) one,
and $\sigma$ the logistic function. If you know chess ratings, this is the same
model as Elo: only the difference between two scores decides who is expected
to win.

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{RM}} = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\right)\right]
$$

Only *differences* of $r_\phi$ within a prompt are constrained, so rewards are
identified only up to an additive function of $x$: add the same $f(x)$ to every
response and nothing changes. Do not read that as "the scale is arbitrary".
Doubling every reward does change the model — $\sigma(1) = 0.731$ against
$\sigma(2) = 0.881$ — unless you rescale the link temperature to match. The
additive freedom is what makes the $Z(x)$ term cancel a few lines from now,
because the offset is the same for both responses to one prompt.

Second, the policy is optimised against that frozen reward, leashed to the
reference:

$$
\max_{\pi_\theta}\; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r_\phi(x, y)\big]
\;-\; \beta\, \mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\!\left[\pi_\theta(y \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\right]
$$

The number $\beta$ is the strength of the leash. A large $\beta$ keeps the
policy close to the reference and gives up some reward; a small $\beta$ lets it
chase the reward further — and, with a learned reward model, closer to reward
hacking.

PPO is one way of taking a step on that objective: it maximises a clipped
surrogate so that a single batch cannot move the policy far
[@schulman2017ppo]. That clip range is one of the hyperparameters the table
below charges to PPO's account.

*That* objective — maximise reward, penalised by KL divergence from the
reference — has a known closed-form optimum:

$$
\pi^{*}(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \, \exp\!\left( \frac{1}{\beta} r(x, y) \right)
$$

Rearrange for $r$:

$$
r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^{*}(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)
$$

[The reward was never a separate object.]{.hl} Any policy already *is* a
reward model, read as its log-ratio against the reference. And the awkward
$Z(x)$ — a sum over every possible response, which is why nobody computes it —
depends only on the prompt, so it cancels the moment you compare two responses
to the *same* prompt. Which is precisely what preference data gives you.

Substituting into the Bradley–Terry model of pairwise preference leaves an
ordinary supervised loss over preference pairs $(x, y_w, y_l)$:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\,\mathbb{E}\left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \right) \right]
$$

Read it in words and it stops being intimidating: *raise the probability of
the preferred answer and lower the probability of the rejected one — but
measure both relative to where the reference model already had them, so you
are rewarded for moving in the right direction rather than for agreeing with
the reference.*

One precision on "raise" and "lower". The loss only asks for the *gap* between
the two log-ratios to widen. In practice both probabilities often fall during
DPO, the rejected one faster, so do not be surprised if the preferred answer's
own likelihood goes down while the loss improves.

Notice what $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is doing here, because it is the reason for the
*"never DPO a base model"* rule you will meet later.

DPO's setup assumes the preference pairs were sampled from the reference. So the
paper sets $\pi_{\text{ref}} = \pi_{\text{SFT}}$ whenever an SFT model
exists — and when one does not, it recommends fine-tuning on the *preferred*
completions first and using that, explicitly "to mitigate the distribution
shift between the true reference distribution which is unavailable, and
$\pi_{\text{ref}}$ used by DPO" [@rafailov2023dpo].

Which locates the failure precisely. [The loss never samples anything. It is
the mismatch between reference and data — not an inability to "rank" — that
breaks DPO on a base model.]{.hl}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**What the substitution actually bought.**

| | RLHF (PPO) | DPO |
|:--|:--|:--|
| models in memory | 4 | 2 (policy + frozen reference) |
| separate reward model | trained first, then kept | none |
| sampling during training | yes, the policy generates every step | no, the pairs are fixed |
| what a step is | a reinforcement-learning update | a gradient step on a classification loss |
| tuning burden | PPO's clip range, value loss, GAE, plus $\beta$ | $\beta$, plus the learning rate |

DPO removed the two things practitioners actually complained about — the
reward model and the generation loop — which is why it went from paper to
default in about a year.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**What DPO did not remove.** Preference pairs are still annotation, and they
are still the expensive part. DPO makes the *algorithm* cheap; the *data* costs
exactly what it did before. It also inherits a subtler problem: because the
pairs are collected once, from some other model's outputs, they go stale as
your policy moves away from whatever generated them. Tülu 3 found that
on-policy preference data — generated by the model being trained — improves
downstream results over reused off-policy pairs [@lambert2025tulu3].
:::

### GRPO: delete the value model instead

DPO deletes the reward model. GRPO [@shao2024deepseekmath] takes the other
route: keep reinforcement learning, but delete the *value* model.

The value model exists to supply a baseline. In policy-gradient methods you do
not want the raw reward — you want to know whether an action was better
**than expected**, because a reward of 8 means something different when your
usual score is 2 than when it is 9. Learning a network to predict that
expectation is the standard answer, and it is expensive: a second trained
model, at the full 16 bytes per parameter.

GRPO's observation is that if you are going to sample from the policy anyway,
you can get a baseline for free. Sample $G$ answers **to the same prompt**,
score them all, and use the group's own mean as the expectation:

$$
A_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}
$$

$A_i$ is called the **advantage** of answer $i$: positive means "better than
this group's average", and the update makes that answer more likely; negative
makes it less likely. Dividing by the standard deviation puts every prompt on
the same scale, so easy and hard prompts pull with comparable force. One
consequence to remember: if all $G$ answers get the same reward — all right or
all wrong — every $A_i$ is zero (implementations add a tiny constant to avoid
dividing by zero), and that prompt teaches nothing.

The question stops being *how good is this answer in absolute terms* and
becomes *was this attempt better than my other attempts at the same question*
— which is both a more stable signal and a free one. GRPO still keeps the
frozen reference and the KL leash, and it still needs *some* reward — a reward
model or, as the next section shows, a checker. In the paper's words (*critic*
is another name for the value model),
GRPO "foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group
scores, significantly reducing training resources" [@shao2024deepseekmath].
On DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B it moved GSM8K from 82.9% to 88.2% and MATH from
46.8% to 51.7%, using only instruction-tuning data already in hand.

### Where the reward comes from, and why that is the real question

There is one more move, and it is the one that changed the field most
recently. Everything above assumed the reward is *learned* — from human
comparisons, so it inherits every flaw of a learned model, including being
gameable.

For some tasks it does not have to be. If the answer is a number, check the
number. If it is code, run the tests. DeepSeek-R1-Zero — the variant trained by
reinforcement learning with no supervised warm-up — uses "rule-based rewards"
of exactly two kinds: **accuracy rewards**, which verify the final answer in a
specified format, and **format rewards**, which check that the reasoning was
placed where it was asked to be [@guo2025deepseekr1]. Tülu 3
builds the same idea into an open recipe under the name **RLVR**, reinforcement
learning with verifiable rewards [@lambert2025tulu3].

::: {.column-margin}
This is also the sharpest limitation. Verifiable rewards need a verifier, and
most things people want from a language model — was this summary faithful, was
this tone appropriate, was this refusal correct — have no verifier. Maths and
code are unusually lucky domains. @sec-reasoning follows what happens
when you push this idea as far as it goes.
:::

The trade is close to clean: a learned reward model covers any task and is easy
to hack; a verifier covers almost nothing and is much harder to hack, but only
as far as its specification and implementation go. A test suite with gaps rewards
a program that hard-codes the visible cases; a loose answer parser rewards
whatever matches its regex (@sec-reasoning has the version of this that bites
in practice). Because the two kinds of reward fail in different ways,
production recipes use both, on different subsets of the data.

### Choosing, by what data you have

Strip the acronyms and every method above is a claim about what you can
collect.

| you have | use | what it costs you |
|:--|:--|:--|
| prompts with ideal answers written out | **SFT** | writing the answers |
| pairs of answers with a "which is better" label | **DPO** | annotation, but not writing |
| the same, plus budget for an RL loop | **RLHF/PPO** | 4 models in memory, unstable, best ceiling on open-ended tasks |
| prompts whose answers can be *checked* | **GRPO + verifiable rewards** | a verifier, and a lot of sampling |
| a stronger model you are allowed to query | **distillation** (@sec-distillation) | inference bills, and a licence question |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The order to try things in, for a team of one or two.** Start with SFT and
stop there. Add DPO only when you have a *specific* complaint about the SFT
model's behaviour that you can express as pairs — "it should have refused
this", "it should have been shorter". Reach for an RL loop only when you have
a verifier, because without one you have just signed up to maintain a reward
model as well as a policy.
:::

## Constitutional AI and feedback that isn't human {#sec-rlaif}

The bottleneck in everything above is annotation. Constitutional AI
[@bai2022constitutional] asks whether the model can supply it.

The method has two halves. In the supervised half, the model answers a
red-team prompt, then **critiques its own answer** against a written
principle, then **revises** it; the revision becomes the training target. In
the RL half, the same principles are used to label preference pairs for
harmlessness, replacing the human annotator there — reinforcement learning
from AI feedback, RLAIF. (In the paper, the helpfulness comparisons were still
labelled by people.)

::: {.column-margin}
Anthropic's team wrote 16 principles for the harmlessness experiments and
sampled one at random at each critique-and-revision step
[@bai2022constitutional]. The randomisation was not for fairness: they found
that ensembling over principles produced notably more robust preference-model
behaviour than using one principle for every label.
:::

Two things about this are worth separating, because they are usually praised
together and only one of them is unambiguous.

**What is clearly good:** the principles are an *artefact*. They are a text
file. You can read them, argue with them, version them, and hand them to a
regulator. Compare that with the alternative, where the model's values are
whatever a few hundred contractors happened to prefer on a Tuesday, recoverable
only by probing the finished model. Moving the specification out of the labels
and into a document is a real gain in accountability, independent of whether
the technique works better.

**What is not settled:** the feedback model has the same blind spots as the
model being trained, because it is often the same model or a close relative
of it. Where it cannot
tell that an answer is subtly wrong, the training signal is confidently wrong,
and no amount of scale fixes a bias shared by both sides of the loop. AI
feedback is at its best on properties a model can check — is this rude, does
this contain the requested section, does this refuse — and at its worst on
properties it would need to be a domain expert to check.

## Distillation into something you can afford {#sec-distillation}

Everything so far has made a model *better*.
[Knowledge distillation](#gloss-knowledge-distillation){#term-knowledge-distillation .term-ref}
[@hinton2015distilling] makes a model *cheaper*, and it is the technique most
often skipped by teams who then complain about their inference bill.

::: {#gloss-knowledge-distillation .column-margin .term-gloss}
**knowledge distillation** — training a small model to reproduce a large one's
outputs. The small model inherits behaviour, not understanding: where the
teacher is wrong, the student learns the mistake rather than correcting it.
[↩](#term-knowledge-distillation){.term-back}
:::

The setup: a large **teacher** produces outputs, a small **student** is trained
to reproduce them. In the classical form the student matches the teacher's
full output distribution — its "soft targets" — which carries far more
information per example than a hard label does. Knowing that the teacher put
70% on *positive*, 25% on *neutral*, and 5% on *negative* tells the student
that this example is borderline; a one-hot label of *positive* does not.

For generative models the modern form is blunter and works well: have the
teacher answer a large set of prompts, filter the answers, and fine-tune the
student on them as ordinary SFT data. DeepSeek-R1's authors did exactly this,
using 800,000 curated samples from their large model to train small dense
models [@guo2025deepseekr1].

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**When a distilled 1B beats a prompted 70B.** Not on capability — on
cost-per-correct-answer. A prompted 70B needs a long instruction prefix on
every call, which it pays for in both latency and tokens; a distilled student
has the instruction baked into its weights and answers from a short prompt. If
your task is narrow and your volume is high, the small model is usually
cheaper per *correct* answer even at a lower accuracy, because you can afford
to run it twice and check.

The condition is narrowness. Distil a general assistant into 1B parameters and
you get a worse general assistant.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Check the licence before you distil.** Many hosted models' terms of service
prohibit using their outputs to train a competing model. This is a contract
question, not a technical one, and it has ended projects late. Open-weight
models differ: some licences explicitly permit it, some require attribution in
the derived model's name.
:::

## Continued pretraining, and the Turkish case {#sec-continued-pretraining}

There is one situation where the "post-training is not a reliable way to add
knowledge" principle genuinely bends: when what is missing is not a fact but a *distribution*. A
model that has seen little Turkish is not missing a fact about Turkish. It is
missing the language.

The tool for that is **continued pretraining**: take the base model and keep
running stage 1 on a domain corpus, with the same next-token objective and no
instruction format at all [@gururangan2020dont]. It sits between the stages —
pretraining's objective, fine-tuning's budget.

::: {#gloss-continued-pretraining .column-margin .term-gloss}
**continued pretraining** — running the pretraining objective again on a
narrower corpus, starting from an existing base model. Used when the gap is a
whole domain or language rather than a task or a format.
[↩](#term-continued-pretraining){.term-back}
:::

For Turkish you have three options, and @sec-tokenizer-budget already priced
one of them for you:

| route | what you get | what it costs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| fine-tune a multilingual model | fastest path; the model already has some Turkish | you pay the tokenizer surcharge on every token, forever |
| [continued pretraining](#gloss-continued-pretraining){#term-continued-pretraining .term-ref} on a Turkish corpus, then SFT | much better Turkish; keeps the base model's world knowledge | tens of billions of tokens; a real, if small, pretraining run |
| start from a Turkish-native model | best fertility, best morphology | small models only; weaker world knowledge and reasoning |

The surcharge in row one is measurable, and we measured it in
@sec-pretraining: Llama 3's tokenizer needs **2.12** tokens per
Turkish word against BERTurk's **1.59**. That is a **33%** longer sequence for
the same text — on every training step, every evaluation, and every user
request until the model is retired. It shows up as a bigger fine-tuning bill,
a smaller effective context window, and higher latency per answer.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The decision rule that survives contact with a budget.** If your task is
classification or extraction and your texts are short, take the Turkish-native
model — you need morphology, not world knowledge, and @sec-lora-lab shows a
110M-parameter one doing very well. If your task needs reasoning or broad
knowledge, take the multilingual model and pay the surcharge, because no
Turkish-native model of the size you can afford has the world model you need.
Continued pretraining is for when you will be running this for years and the
surcharge has become the dominant line item.
:::

## When not to fine-tune {#sec-decision-tree}

Most of this chapter has been about how. This section is about *whether*, and
it is the part to remember if you remember one part.

The failure mode is specific and common. A team has a model that gets things
wrong about their business. Fine-tuning is the technique that sounds like
"teach the model about our business". They collect examples, run a LoRA job,
and the model comes back **more fluent and just as wrong** — because they
taught it the *style* of their documentation while the *contents* of their
documentation were never in the gradient in any retrievable form.
